title: How many squares are there in each step?
description: A pattern of squares starts with five squares and gains four squares at every step. The count is four n plus one, which gives seventeen, forty one and two hundred and one, and the vertices follow as sixteen n plus four.
teaching_notes: One idea: the first step has five squares and every later step adds four, so step n adds four n minus one times. Watch for students who write four n or five n.

video_script.why: A learner uses the method of the bracket formula: the first step is counted once and each later step adds the same amount, written with a bracket and then opened.
video_script.substitution: The method of three plus two times the bracket y minus one, with five plus four times the bracket n minus one for the squares.
video_script.anchor: a pattern of squares that grows with each step
video_script.payoff_line: Steps four, ten and fifty have seventeen, forty one and two hundred and one squares

final_answer.value: 17, 41 and 201 squares; the formula is 4n + 1; vertices 16n + 4
final_answer.spoken: seventeen, forty one and two hundred and one squares; the formula is four n plus one; the vertices are sixteen n plus four

hold_back: Answer: 17, 41 and 201 squares; the formula is 4n + 1; vertices 16n + 4
never_show: the finished formula before the answer beat
maths_rules: step 1 has 5 squares and each step adds 4, so step n has 5 + (n - 1) x 4 squares
each square has 4 vertices, counted separately: 4 x (4n + 1) = 16n + 4
video_script.design: One idea: five squares to start and four more at each step, written with a bracket and then opened. Assumes the example of a count with a bracket. The first three steps stay on the stage.
open_questions: The picture is not in the extracted book text, so the video follows the worklist. The vertex count 16n + 4 counts the four vertices of every square separately, with no shared corners merged.

narration: <bookmark mark='fd'/>We find the squares, then the formula, then the vertices. We work the same way as the example in your book.

marks.s1a: step n is shown as step one plus n − 1 additions

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>First, step n comes after n minus one additions of four squares.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>The count is five plus the bracket n minus one, times four.
<bookmark mark='s2a'/>Second, open the bracket. Four times the bracket n minus one is four n minus four.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>Five minus four is one, so the formula is four n plus one.
<bookmark mark='s3a'/>Third, step four gives four times four plus one, which is seventeen squares.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Step ten gives four times ten plus one, which is forty one squares.
<bookmark mark='s3c'/>Step fifty gives four times fifty plus one, which is two hundred and one squares.

beats.on_screen: Fourth: each square has 4 vertices ; vertices = 4 × (4n + 1) = 16n + 4

marks.s4a: four vertices are marked on one square

narration: <bookmark mark='s4a'/>Fourth, every square has four vertices, and we count them for each square separately.
<bookmark mark='s4b'/>The vertices are four times the bracket four n plus one, which is sixteen n plus four.

marks.s5b: the formula 16n + 4 with n as 4 also gives 68

narration: <bookmark mark='s5a'/>Fifth, check step four. Seventeen squares have four times seventeen vertices, which is sixty eight.
<bookmark mark='s5b'/>Sixteen times four plus four is also sixty eight.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 17, 41 and 201 squares; the formula is 4n + 1; vertices 16n + 4
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Steps four, ten and fifty have seventeen, forty one and two hundred and one squares.
<bookmark mark='ans2'/>Step n has four n plus one squares, and sixteen n plus four vertices.
